novel_features.name: Fleet rollup
novel_features.description: See core version, pending updates, admin-account count and sync age for every site you manage, in one table.
novel_features.rationale: WordPress has no concept of a fleet — there is no endpoint for 'all my sites'. Requires a cross-site join over per-site-keyed local stores.
novel_features.why_it_matters: Reach for this when the question spans more than one site. Every other command answers for a single site.

novel_features.name: REST reachability diagnosis
novel_features.description: Say in one command why a site's REST API is failing: path-based block, app-layer filter, bot challenge, renamed prefix, or stripped Authorization header.
novel_features.rationale: A probe of 39 live WordPress sites found 36% do not answer /wp-json on the first try, and 18% recover only via the ?rest_route= fallback. Classification needs four probes plus a transport fallback that no other tool performs.
novel_features.why_it_matters: Run this first whenever a WordPress request fails. A 401 can mean bad credentials, a security plugin, or a host stripping the auth header, and the status code alone cannot tell you which.

novel_features.name: Credential capability audit
novel_features.description: Report what your credentials are actually allowed to do on each route, with zero writes.
novel_features.rationale: WordPress's Allow response header reflects the current credential's permissions per route, so walking the live route table with and without auth yields a full permission map without mutating anything. No competitor reads this header.
novel_features.why_it_matters: Use this before pointing an unattended job at a site, instead of discovering permissions by attempting a write in production.

novel_features.name: REST visibility gap
novel_features.description: Find out why a post type, field, or meta key is missing from the REST surface.
novel_features.rationale: Set-differences the types registry against the live route table and the OPTIONS property schema against actual synced rows. Both abandoned Go clients model post types as fixed structs and silently drop custom ones.
novel_features.why_it_matters: This is the show_in_rest blind spot. Reach for it when content exists in wp-admin but never appears in an API response.

novel_features.name: Editorial queue with age
novel_features.description: See drafts, pending, and scheduled posts bucketed by how long they have been sitting in that state.
novel_features.rationale: The API returns rows, not durations, and never across three statuses at once. Requires local duration math over synced timestamps.
novel_features.why_it_matters: Answers 'what has been stuck in pending for three weeks', which wp-admin cannot express at all.
novel_features.group: Editorial hygiene from the local mirror

novel_features.name: Content hygiene audit
novel_features.description: Find posts and pages missing a featured image, a real category, an excerpt, or tags.
novel_features.rationale: Four completeness checks, three of which need a join across posts, media, and term links that the REST API cannot express in any single call.
novel_features.why_it_matters: Use this for defects on content itself. It reports offending IDs, so the output feeds directly into a bulk fix.
novel_features.group: Editorial hygiene from the local mirror

novel_features.name: Orphaned media
novel_features.description: List media files that no post or page references and that are nobody's featured image.
novel_features.rationale: WordPress has no unused-media endpoint. Requires scanning synced content for each media item's source URL and cross-checking featured_media.
novel_features.why_it_matters: Reach for this when auditing storage or preparing a migration; it is the only way to size unused uploads without shell access.
novel_features.group: Editorial hygiene from the local mirror

narrative.headline: WP-CLI-grade control over any WordPress site through plain HTTPS — no SSH, no server-side plugin, one static binary.
narrative.value_prop: WP-CLI is the power tool but it runs on the server and needs SSH, which most shared hosting does not give you. The REST API reaches any site from anywhere with an Application Password, yet every existing client is abandoned, read-only, or hardcoded to a 2018 view of the API. This CLI covers the full modern core surface, adapts to the live route table of whatever site you point it at, and keeps a local SQLite mirror so cross-site and historical questions become one query instead of hundreds of paginated requests.
narrative.auth_narrative: WordPress authenticates CLI clients with Application Passwords over HTTP Basic. Create one at Users -> Profile -> Application Passwords in wp-admin (the REST root also advertises the exact authorize-application.php URL for the site), then set WORDPRESS_USER and WORDPRESS_APP_PASSWORD. Public read endpoints work with no credentials at all, so posts, pages, and taxonomies are browsable immediately. Two things commonly break this and neither is a wrong password: Wordfence disables Application Passwords by default on its 5,000,000+ installs, and many Apache and CGI hosts strip the Authorization header entirely. Run 'diagnose' to tell those apart.

public reads need no credentials, so this works with zero configuration
the first thing to run against any new site — says whether REST is reachable and, if not, exactly why
what your credentials may actually do here, discovered without a single write
build the local mirror; incremental via modified_after, not a full re-pull
what is stuck in the editorial pipeline and for how long

troubleshoots.symptom: 401 rest_forbidden even though the password is correct
troubleshoots.fix: Run 'wordpress-pp-cli diagnose'. The usual causes are Wordfence disabling Application Passwords site-side or the host stripping the Authorization header; the site-health authorization-header test distinguishes them.
Permalinks are set to Plain, or an edge rule blocks the literal path. Both are handled by the ?rest_route= fallback, which 'diagnose' probes automatically.

troubleshoots.symptom: 403 with an HTML body instead of JSON
troubleshoots.fix: A bot-mitigation layer (commonly Cloudflare) is challenging the request above WordPress. This cannot be fixed client-side; the site owner must allowlist the path.
Read data.details in the JSON error — it names the offending parameter and the accepted range. per_page is hard-capped at 100.

troubleshoots.symptom: A custom post type or ACF field never appears in responses
troubleshoots.fix: It was registered without show_in_rest. Run 'wordpress-pp-cli schema <type>' to see exactly which declared fields never carry data.

troubleshoots.symptom: Editing a page turns it into one invalid block in the editor
troubleshoots.fix: Never write back content.rendered. Read with --context edit to get content.raw, which preserves the block markers, and write that.
Hosts and WAFs began blocking /wp-json/batch/v1 after CVE-2026-63030. Update WordPress to 6.9.5 or 7.0.2 and ask the host to allowlist the route, or let the command fall back to sequential requests.

narrative.when_to_use: Use this CLI to read from or write to any WordPress site over HTTPS when you have a site URL and an Application Password. It is the right tool for content operations at scale (bulk publishing, editorial queue triage, taxonomy and media hygiene), for fleet maintenance across many client sites without SSH, and for diagnosing a WordPress REST API that is returning 401, 403, or rest_no_route. It is also the right tool when you need to know what a site's API actually exposes, since it reads the live route table rather than assuming a fixed endpoint list.
anti_triggers: Do not use this CLI for database work — export, import, search-replace, or arbitrary SQL. WordPress exposes none of that over REST; use WP-CLI over SSH.
Do not use it to install, update, or activate a theme. The core themes controller is read-only over REST; theme activation is not possible, and tools that advertise it are overclaiming.
Do not use it to read or write arbitrary options. The settings endpoint exposes roughly twenty whitelisted core options under renamed keys; anything else needs register_setting with show_in_rest.
Do not use it for WP-Cron, transients, object cache, rewrite rules, wp-config.php, roles and capabilities, or multisite network administration — none have a core REST surface.
Do not use it to round-trip block-editor content through content.rendered; that strips the block markers and corrupts the page. Use --context edit and content.raw.
Do not use it as a WordPress.com or Jetpack client. This targets the self-hosted /wp-json surface.

recipes.title: Triage a site that just started failing
recipes.explanation: Classifies the failure as a path-based block, an app-layer filter, a bot challenge, a renamed REST prefix, or a stripped Authorization header, instead of leaving you with a bare 401.

recipes.title: Pull only the fields you need from a verbose endpoint
recipes.explanation: WordPress post objects carry 29 properties plus embedded links; narrowing with --select keeps large listings from flooding an agent's context.

recipes.title: Check what a credential may do before automating with it
recipes.explanation: Walks the live route table reading the Allow header with and without authentication, so permissions are discovered without performing a single write.

recipes.title: Find content defects across a synced site
recipes.explanation: Joins posts against media and term links locally to report missing featured images, categories, excerpts, and tags with the offending IDs.

recipes.title: See what this specific site actually exposes
recipes.explanation: Reconciles the post-types registry, the live route table, and the OPTIONS schema against real rows, surfacing fields registered without show_in_rest.
